study.title: Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised.
study.intro: Fourteen verses praise God in His city: Zion's beauty, kings who fled in terror, ships wrecked by an east wind, and an invitation to walk the walls and tell the next generation.
study.context: The heading calls this a song and a Psalm of the sons of Korah. It is one of the 'Songs of Zion' (with Psalms 46, 76, 84, 87 and 122). Verses 1–3 praise Zion; verses 4–8 tell of allied kings who advanced, saw and fled, with an east wind wrecking the ships of Tarshish; verses 9–11 meditate on God's love in the temple; verses 12–14 invite worshipers to walk around the city and tell the next generation. No battle is named; many connect it with Jerusalem's rescue from Assyria (2 Kings 19). 'Zaphon' in verse 2 was the northern mountain of Canaanite myth, so the psalm claims for Zion the honor others gave their gods' mountain. Verse 2 is echoed by Jesus in Matthew 5:35. The Scripture is loaded unchanged from the bundled BSB, including the heading.
study.peopleNote: The heading credits this Song of Zion to the sons of Korah. No other person is named. Planned paintings show Jerusalem's walls, towers, ships and pilgrims from a distance; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: Greatly to be praised
verses.heading: God in His holy mountain
verses.meaning: The heading calls this a song of the sons of Korah. It opens with praise: the LORD is great and deserves great praise. The place of praise is His city, His holy mountain, Zion. The psalm celebrates God through the place where He chose to dwell. The focus remains on God, not merely the buildings. Jerusalem matters because God is praised there.
verses.context: Psalm 145:3 says, 'Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised,' and Psalm 87:1–3 celebrates Zion as founded on the holy mountain. Psalm 48 belongs to the 'Songs of Zion' group.
explore: Greatly to be praised
Praise should match God's greatness. Small praise is too small for Him.
His holy mountain
Zion is set apart. It is not the stone that makes it holy but God's presence there.
verses.reflect: How great is God to you today? How could your praise reflect that?
verses.alt: Jerusalem's walls glow on a mountain at golden hour.

verses.title: Joy of all the earth
verses.heading: Zion's beauty and height
verses.meaning: Beautiful in loftiness, the joy of all the earth, like the peaks of Zaphon is Mount Zion, the city of the great King. Zion is praised as beautiful and high. In fact it was not tall compared to nearby hills, so its height is spiritual. Zaphon was the sacred northern mountain of Canaanite myth, home of Baal. The psalm claims that Zion, not Zaphon, is the true dwelling of the great King. Jesus calls Jerusalem 'the city of the great King' in Matthew 5:35.
verses.context: Isaiah 14:13 refers to the 'mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north (Zaphon),' and Matthew 5:35 echoes 'city of the great King.' Psalm 48:2 gives Zion the honor others gave Zaphon.
explore: Beautiful in loftiness
Zion's height is a matter of honor, not geography. God's presence lifts it.
City of the great King
The title belongs to God. Jesus repeated it in His teaching.
verses.reflect: What makes a place beautiful in your eyes? How might God's presence change that?
verses.alt: A mountain city rises above clouds like a sacred peak.

verses.title: God in her citadels
verses.heading: A proven fortress
verses.meaning: God is in her citadels; He has shown Himself to be a fortress. The city's real defense is God. Citadels were the strongest towers of the city, but God is within them. He has 'shown Himself' or 'made Himself known' as a fortress, meaning He has proved it in history. Confidence comes from experience. The next verses tell the story.
verses.context: Psalm 46:7 calls the God of Jacob our fortress, and Proverbs 18:10 says the name of the LORD is a strong tower. Psalm 48:3 says God has proved it.
explore: In her citadels
God is in the strongest towers. Walls alone do not protect.
Shown Himself
God's protection is proven. It is known from experience.
verses.reflect: When has God shown Himself to be your fortress in a hard season?
verses.alt: A massive corner tower of a city wall stands in clear light.

verses.title: The kings assembled
verses.heading: An alliance advances
verses.meaning: For behold, the kings assembled; they all advanced together. The story begins. Kings joined forces and marched together against the city. 'Behold' calls for attention. The alliance seems unstoppable. No specific kings are named, which allows the psalm to celebrate a pattern of deliverance. The tension builds for the next verse.
verses.context: Psalm 2:2 describes kings setting themselves against the LORD, and 2 Kings 18–19 recounts the Assyrian army advancing on Jerusalem. Psalm 48:4 tells of an alliance coming against Zion.
explore: Behold
The listener is asked to look. Something remarkable is coming.
Advanced together
The kings combine their forces. The threat to the city seems overwhelming.
verses.reflect: What forces seem to be advancing against you? How do you see them?
verses.alt: Many banners of allied armies rise over a distant ridge.

verses.title: They fled in terror
verses.heading: Astounded at the sight
verses.meaning: They saw and were astounded; they fled in terror. The story turns quickly. The kings looked at the city, perhaps sensing God's presence, and were stunned. Then they fled. The three verbs move fast: saw, astounded, fled. The psalm suggests that the sight of God's city with God in it was enough to scatter them. Victory is God's, not Israel's.
verses.context: The quick sequence 'saw... were astounded... fled' shows a collapse without battle. Exodus 15:14–16 describes nations trembling at God's acts, and 2 Kings 19:36 records Sennacherib withdrawing.
explore: They saw
The kings saw something. God's presence was evident.
Fled in terror
The alliance collapses at once. Without a battle, the kings run away.
verses.reflect: When have you seen fears dissolve in the presence of God?
verses.alt: Dust trails stretch away from a city as distant armies retreat.

verses.title: Anguish like labor
verses.heading: Trembling seized them
verses.meaning: Trembling seized them there, anguish like a woman in labor. The fleeing kings are described as gripped by trembling. The image of a woman in labor was a common biblical picture of sudden, overwhelming pain. It shows helplessness: the kings cannot stop what is happening to them. The verse emphasizes how complete their fear is.
verses.context: Isaiah 13:8 and Jeremiah 6:24 use labor pains to describe terror, and 1 Thessalonians 5:3 uses it of sudden destruction. Psalm 48:6 applies it to the fleeing kings.
explore: Trembling seized them
Fear grips the kings where they stand. They cannot resist or control it.
Like a woman in labor
The image is sudden and intense. It shows helplessness.
verses.reflect: What would it mean for fear to be replaced by trust in you?
verses.alt: Abandoned crowns and helmets lie on a hillside in morning mist.

verses.title: Ships of Tarshish
verses.heading: Wrecked by an east wind
verses.meaning: With a wind from the east You wrecked the ships of Tarshish. A new image appears: God breaks great ships with an east wind. Tarshish ships were large ocean-going vessels, symbols of power and wealth. The east wind was a strong, dry, destructive wind. The image may be a comparison: as God wrecks mighty ships, so He scattered the kings. It shows God's power over the sea and its strongest vessels.
verses.context: Exodus 14:21 records God driving back the sea with a strong east wind, and Isaiah 2:16 names the ships of Tarshish among symbols of pride. Jonah 1:3–4 describes a Tarshish-bound ship caught in a storm.
explore: Wind from the east
The east wind off the desert was powerful and dry. God commands even it.
Ships of Tarshish
Great ocean-going ships symbolized wealth and power. God breaks them easily.
verses.reflect: What powerful things in the world seem unbreakable? How do they look before God?
verses.alt: Tall-masted ships break apart on a stormy sea driven by a violent wind.

verses.title: As we have heard, so we have seen
verses.heading: Stories confirmed by sight
verses.meaning: As we have heard, so we have seen in the city of the LORD of Hosts, in the city of our God: God will establish her forever. Selah. The people had heard stories of God's protection. Now they have seen it with their own eyes. Faith inherited through hearing has been confirmed by experience. The conclusion is that God will establish the city forever. Selah invites reflection. The verse contrasts with Psalm 44, where present experience contradicted what the fathers had told.
verses.context: Job 42:5 says, 'My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You,' and Psalm 44:1 recalls what the fathers told. Psalm 48:8 finds those stories confirmed.
explore: As we have heard
The stories passed down are true. Hearing is confirmed.
Establish her forever
God's commitment to Zion is lasting. Selah marks the confidence.
verses.reflect: Where has what you heard about God been confirmed in your experience?
verses.alt: A grandfather and child stand on a wall gazing at the city.

verses.title: Within Your temple
verses.heading: Contemplating loving devotion
verses.meaning: Within Your temple, O God, we contemplate Your loving devotion. After the drama of verses 4–8, the scene becomes quiet. In the temple the worshipers reflect on God's loving devotion, His covenant faithfulness. To contemplate means to ponder, to think over carefully. Deliverance leads to meditation on God's character. The verse shows that worship includes thoughtful reflection, not just celebration.
verses.context: Psalm 27:4 seeks to gaze on the LORD's beauty in His temple, and Psalm 77:12 says, 'I will reflect on all You have done.' Psalm 48:9 brings that reflection into the temple.
explore: Contemplate
The word means to ponder. Worship includes thought.
Loving devotion
God's covenant love is the focus. Deliverance reveals it.
verses.reflect: Where could you quietly ponder God's loving devotion this week?
verses.alt: A quiet temple court with a single bench and lamps at evening.

verses.title: To the ends of the earth
verses.heading: God's name and righteous right hand
verses.meaning: Your name, O God, like Your praise, reaches to the ends of the earth; Your right hand is full of righteousness. God's reputation and praise extend far beyond Jerusalem. His name, meaning His character, is known everywhere. His right hand, symbol of power, is full of righteousness. His power is always just. The verse widens the view from the temple to the world.
verses.context: Malachi 1:11 says God's name will be great among the nations, and Psalm 113:3 says from the rising of the sun to its setting the LORD's name is to be praised. Psalm 48:10 sees God's praise reach the ends of the earth.
explore: Ends of the earth
God's praise is global. It is not limited to Israel.
Full of righteousness
God's power is always just. His strength serves what is right.
verses.reflect: How does knowing God's power is full of righteousness give you confidence?
verses.alt: A coastline at sunset stretches far to a distant horizon.

verses.title: Daughters of Judah rejoice
verses.heading: Gladness at God's judgments
verses.meaning: Mount Zion is glad, the daughters of Judah rejoice, on account of Your judgments. The city and the towns of Judah rejoice. 'Daughters of Judah' likely means the surrounding villages. They celebrate God's judgments, meaning His acts of justice in defending them. Judgment here is good news for the oppressed. It means God has set things right.
verses.context: Psalm 97:8 says, 'Zion hears and rejoices, and the towns of Judah exult because of Your judgments.' Psalm 96:12–13 pictures creation rejoicing because God comes to judge.
explore: Daughters of Judah
The towns of Judah join the joy. The celebration spreads.
Your judgments
God's justice brings gladness. He has made things right.
verses.reflect: Where do you long to see God's justice? How could you rejoice in it?
verses.alt: Villagers dance with tambourines in a hillside town square.

verses.title: Count her towers
verses.heading: An invitation to walk around Zion
verses.meaning: March around Zion, encircle her, count her towers. The worshipers are invited to walk around the city. They should count the towers, a way of seeing that the city still stands after the threat. The action is like a pilgrim's tour. It turns faith into something seen and touched. The invitation continues in verse 13.
verses.context: Nehemiah 12:31–40 records a dedication procession around Jerusalem's walls, and Joshua 6 records a march around Jericho with a very different purpose. Psalm 48:12 invites a joyful tour.
explore: March around
The worshipers walk the circuit. It is an act of celebration.
Count her towers
The towers still stand. Counting confirms God's protection.
verses.reflect: What evidence of God's faithfulness could you 'count' in your life?
verses.alt: Pilgrims walk the top of a long city wall counting towers.

verses.title: Tell the next generation
verses.heading: Ramparts and citadels as testimony
verses.meaning: Consider her ramparts, tour her citadels, that you may tell the next generation. The tour has a purpose: to tell those who come after. Ramparts and citadels are evidence of God's protection. The worshipers are to take careful note so they can pass on the story. Faith is meant to be handed down. The verse connects worship with teaching.
verses.context: Psalm 78:4–6 speaks of telling the next generation the LORD's deeds, and Joshua 4:6–7 gives stones as a sign for children to ask about. Psalm 48:13 turns the city into a lesson.
explore: Consider her ramparts
Look carefully at the walls. The details are evidence of God's protection.
Tell the next generation
The purpose of the tour is teaching. Faith must be passed on to children.
verses.reflect: What story of God's faithfulness could you tell someone younger this week?
verses.alt: A father shows his son the massive base stones of a rampart.

verses.title: Our guide even till death
verses.heading: This God is our God forever
verses.meaning: For this God is our God forever and ever; He will be our guide even till death. The psalm ends with its point. The walls and towers are not the final security. 'This God,' the One who defended the city, is our God forever. He will guide us even until death. The final phrase is personal. The God of the city is a shepherd who leads His people through all of life.
verses.context: Psalm 23:4 says God is with us in the valley of the shadow, and Isaiah 58:11 says, 'The LORD will always guide you.' Psalm 48:14 ends the tour of the walls with God Himself as guide.
explore: This God
The God who acted is our God. The walls point to Him.
Guide even till death
God leads all through life. His guidance does not stop.
verses.reflect: What would it mean for you to know God as your guide until the end of life?
verses.alt: A shepherd's staff leans against a gate opening onto a long road.
